passage: In the school library during free period, Tanish, nine, was halfway through a jigsaw of a sailing ship when the bell rang for PE. He left three corner pieces on the table. All through the football game he kept thinking about the missing blue piece of the sky. He even missed a pass. When the bell rang again, he ran straight back to the library, found the piece and pressed it in. He sighed happily. Later, when his mother asked about the maths sheet he had finished that morning, he could not remember a single question.

qa.q: What was the jigsaw a picture of?
qa.a: A sailing ship.

qa.q: Why did Tanish keep thinking about the puzzle during PE?
qa.a: The unfinished puzzle felt open and nagging, so his mind kept going back to it. 🤔

qa.q: How could Tanish use this pattern for his homework?
qa.a: He could stop a task at an interesting point so his mind stays drawn to finishing it, or finish small tasks fully to stop them nagging.

qa.q: How might his PE teammates see Tanish during the game?
qa.a: They might think he was distracted or not trying, since he missed a pass.

grounding: It shows a child whose unfinished puzzle keeps nagging while his finished work slips from mind.

passage: My younger brother Neil is ten. Last Sunday he was building a Lego bridge when Mum called him for lunch. He came, but he ate fast and kept looking toward his room. He asked twice if he could go back. I don't know exactly what was in his head, but he seemed restless. After lunch he rushed back and finished it in ten minutes. Then he forgot about it completely and didn't even show Dad. It was like the bridge only mattered while it was unfinished.

qa.q: What was Neil building?
qa.a: A Lego bridge.

qa.q: What does Neil's restlessness at lunch most likely show?
qa.a: Most likely his unfinished bridge kept pulling at his attention; his sibling cannot be sure what he was thinking.

qa.q: How could the family use this pattern?
qa.a: They could give Neil a warning before meals so he can reach a stopping point, making it easier to leave. 🙂

qa.q: How did the sibling view Neil forgetting the bridge?
qa.a: They found it strange that the bridge mattered so much only while unfinished.

grounding: It illustrates a child's unfinished task holding his attention until it is complete.

passage: Before: On Friday, Aisha, eleven, was halfway through drawing a comic strip when her father said it was time for bed. During: She lay awake thinking about the last panel. What would the cat say? She got up twice to look at it. On Saturday morning, before breakfast, she finished it. After: By Sunday, she could not even remember what the finished comic said. But the unfinished science worksheet in her bag kept popping into her head until she did it.

qa.q: What was Aisha drawing?
qa.a: A comic strip.

qa.q: Why did Aisha lie awake thinking about the comic?
qa.a: The unfinished last panel felt open, so her mind kept returning to it. 😅

qa.q: How could Aisha use this pattern well?
qa.a: She could finish tasks before bed or write down where she stopped, so they do not keep her awake.

qa.q: How might her father see Aisha getting up twice?
qa.a: He might think she was restless or not tired, not knowing the comic was on her mind.

grounding: It shows a child's unfinished drawing holding her attention, while finished tasks are forgotten.

passage: In a small town in Karnataka, twenty-year-old Deepa brought home a new medicine for her skin. She unfolded the long leaflet and read every line: headache, dizziness, stomach upset, tiredness. That evening she felt a slight headache. Then a twinge in her stomach. "It's starting," she told her sister, heart pounding. Her sister asked if she had eaten lunch. She had not. After dinner, the headache faded. Still, the stomach feeling stayed for three days, so Deepa went back to the doctor to check it properly.

qa.q: What was the new medicine for?
qa.a: For Deepa's skin.

qa.q: Why did Deepa feel sure the side effects were starting?
qa.a: After reading the long list, fear made her notice each small feeling as a listed effect. 😰

qa.q: What did Deepa do well in the end?
qa.a: She went back to the doctor when the stomach feeling lasted three days, instead of just ignoring or panicking.

qa.q: How might her sister see Deepa's worry?
qa.a: Her sister seemed calm and looked for simple reasons, like skipping lunch.

grounding: It shows a young adult noticing twinges as listed side effects after reading a leaflet, while still checking a lasting symptom.

passage: In a student flat in Madrid, Lucía, nineteen, got a new allergy medicine. She read the leaflet twice. By bedtime she felt her heart racing and her hands tingling, both on the list. She searched online and felt worse. Her flatmate Sofía sat with her. "You were fine an hour ago. Did the tingling start after you read it?" Lucía paused. "Maybe." They breathed slowly together, and the racing eased. But she decided to call the clinic in the morning anyway, just to be sure.

qa.q: What kind of medicine did Lucía get?
qa.a: A new allergy medicine.

qa.q: Why did Lucía feel worse after searching online?
qa.a: Reading more about the effects made her more afraid, and fear magnified what she felt.

qa.q: What was wise about Lucía's plan?
qa.a: She calmed down with her flatmate but still planned to call the clinic, not dismissing her symptoms. 🙏

qa.q: How did Sofía see the situation?
qa.a: She gently wondered if reading the list had triggered the feelings, and stayed with Lucía.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult's fear after reading side effects magnifying symptoms, while still seeking proper care.

passage: In the college health centre waiting room, twenty-one-year-old Arjun held the leaflet from his new tablets. A fellow student beside him said, "Those made my cousin dizzy." Arjun started reading every possible effect. Within minutes, the room felt too bright and his head felt light. He told the nurse he was getting side effects already. She asked, "Have you taken the first one yet?" He hadn't. Arjun laughed, embarrassed. The nurse said it was fine to ask, and to come back if anything lasted.

qa.q: What had the fellow student said about the tablets?
qa.a: That they made his cousin dizzy.

qa.q: Why did Arjun feel dizzy before taking any tablet?
qa.a: Hearing the story and reading the effects made him afraid, and the fear created or magnified the feelings. 😅

qa.q: What did the nurse do well?
qa.a: She gently checked the facts, did not mock him, and told him to come back if anything lasted.

qa.q: How might the fellow student see Arjun's reaction?
qa.a: They may not have realised their comment worried him so much.

grounding: It shows fear from side-effect information making a young adult notice symptoms, with a nurse advising follow-up.

passage: Clinic nurse's note. Mr. Farhan, twenty-five, came for his follow-up. He told me he felt hopeful about the new treatment and that the hope helped him sleep. He also said he had read online that the medicine might cause mood changes, and that worried him. I was glad he told us. The doctor explained what was common and what was rare, in plain words. He asked sensible questions. He said he would keep a short diary and call if any symptom lasted more than a few days. I have booked him in for next month.

qa.q: What did Mr. Farhan say he would keep?
qa.a: A short diary.

qa.q: How was Mr. Farhan feeling about the treatment?
qa.a: Hopeful, which helped him sleep, but also worried about possible mood changes.

qa.q: What did Mr. Farhan do well?
qa.a: He told the doctor his worries, asked for balanced information and planned to report lasting symptoms. 👍

qa.q: How did the nurse see Mr. Farhan sharing his worry?
qa.a: She was glad he told them, since it let the doctor explain properly.

grounding: It shows an adult welcoming hope while sharing worries with the doctor and not dismissing lasting symptoms.

passage: Journal, 3 July. Started the physiotherapy plan today. I really believe it will help, and honestly, that belief makes me want to do the exercises. But I'm not going to pretend my knee is fine just because I'm positive. Last time I ignored pain for weeks and it got worse. I told the physio I'm nervous about the swelling coming back. She explained what's normal soreness and what isn't. I wrote both lists on my phone. If the swelling lasts more than two days, I call her. Hopeful, but not blind.

qa.q: What did the writer write on their phone?
qa.a: Both lists: normal soreness and what isn't normal.

qa.q: How does the writer feel about the physiotherapy?
qa.a: Hopeful and motivated, but also nervous about the swelling coming back. 🙂

qa.q: What did the writer do differently from last time?
qa.a: They shared their worry, asked what is normal, and set a clear point to call the physio instead of ignoring pain.

qa.q: How might the physio see the writer's approach?
qa.a: She would likely appreciate that the writer is positive but also careful to report problems.

grounding: It illustrates an adult using hopeful expectation while asking for balanced information and not ignoring symptoms.

qa.q: How does Kabir see Riya's choices?

passage: Teacher's note, UKG. I realised this week that I smile more at Aarav because on the first day I thought he seemed bright. I give him extra time to answer and praise his tries. He now raises his hand every day and keeps trying hard puzzles. But I noticed Priya, who is quiet, gets less of my time. Today I sat with her, waited for her answer, and smiled. She looked surprised, then tried the next puzzle too. I will try to give every child that same warmth.

qa.q: Who did the teacher sit with today?
qa.a: She sat with Priya.

qa.q: How did Priya seem to feel when the teacher waited and smiled?
qa.a: She looked surprised, then tried the next puzzle, suggesting she felt encouraged. 🙂

qa.q: How could the teacher use this insight?
qa.a: By giving every child extra time, warmth and belief, so all of them feel trying is worthwhile.

qa.q: How does Aarav experience the teacher's warmth?
qa.a: He feels capable, so he raises his hand every day and keeps trying hard puzzles.

grounding: It shows a child called bright receiving more warmth and beginning to act bright, and a teacher noticing this.

passage: In a village school near Udaipur, the new teacher told the class, "Meena is very clever." Meena, five, was not sure why. But the teacher smiled at her often and asked her to read the alphabet chart aloud. Meena practised at home by the lamp, reading to her goats. By the end of the month, she was reading faster than anyone. When her friend asked how she got so good, Meena shrugged. "Teacher says I'm clever," she said, beaming.

qa.q: What did Meena read at home by the lamp?
qa.a: She practised reading, reading to her goats.

qa.q: Why did Meena practise so much?
qa.a: Being treated as clever made trying feel worthwhile, so she wanted to live up to it. 😊

qa.q: What could the teacher do so other children benefit too?
qa.a: Show the same belief and warmth to every child, not only Meena.

qa.q: How might Meena's friend feel hearing that the teacher called her clever?
qa.a: The friend might wish the teacher believed in them the same way.

grounding: It illustrates a child being treated as bright by a teacher and beginning to act bright.

passage: In a small school in Auckland, Mrs. Taylor told Leo, five, "You're a great builder." After that, she often came to see his block towers and asked him questions. Leo started building taller and trickier towers. He even helped other children when their towers fell. At pick-up, his dad asked why he liked school so much now. Leo said, "Mrs. Taylor thinks I'm good at building." He ran back to show his dad the tallest tower yet.

qa.q: What did Mrs. Taylor tell Leo?
qa.a: She told Leo he was a great builder.

qa.q: Why did Leo start building taller and trickier towers?
qa.a: Being treated as capable made trying hard feel worthwhile for him. 😊

qa.q: How could Mrs. Taylor spread this effect?
qa.a: She could notice and praise each child's efforts so all feel capable.

qa.q: How might Leo's dad feel hearing this?
qa.a: He would likely feel happy and grateful that the teacher's belief made Leo enjoy school.

grounding: It shows a child whom the teacher calls capable getting more attention and beginning to act capable.

subtype: Family verdict about who they will become [Receiver]
passage: The results would come out in two days, and the house was already tense because Papa had lost his job. At dinner, Aunt Sunita said again to fifteen-year-old Rohit, "You'll never be like your cousin Arjun. He's a topper." Rohit stared at his plate. He had stopped trying in maths months ago. Why bother, if he was the one who would never be like Arjun? Later, his mother came to his room. "I've seen you work hard when you care. I believe in your effort, not your marks." Rohit said nothing, but that night he opened his maths book again.

qa.q: What did Aunt Sunita say at dinner?
qa.a: She said Rohit would never be like his cousin Arjun, the topper.

qa.q: Why had Rohit stopped trying in maths?
qa.a: He had slowly started believing the family verdict that he would never be like Arjun, so trying felt pointless. 😔

qa.q: What did his mother do that could help?
qa.a: She showed steady belief in his effort, not his marks, which quietly lifted him.

qa.q: How might Aunt Sunita see her comments?
qa.a: She may think she is only stating facts or motivating him, not realising they shape his identity.

grounding: It shows a teen absorbing a family verdict comparing him to a cousin, and a parent's belief in effort lifting him.

subtype: Family verdict about who they will become [Receiver]
passage: In their Chennai flat, sixteen-year-old Nila heard it again at the family function. "Nila is the lazy one. Her cousin Divya is the smart one." Everyone laughed. Nila laughed too. At home, she threw her bag on the bed. She did not even try in the drawing competition this year. What was the point? Her father knocked on the door. "You worked on that drawing for three weeks last year. I saw it. That's not lazy." Nila looked up. For the first time in weeks, she took out her sketchbook.

qa.q: What did relatives call Nila at the function?
qa.a: The lazy one.

qa.q: Why did Nila laugh at the function even though it hurt?
qa.a: She may have been hiding her hurt, and slowly accepting the label as who she is.

qa.q: What did Nila's father do well?

qa.q: How might the relatives see their joke?
qa.a: They may see it as harmless teasing, not realising Nila is taking it as her identity.

grounding: It illustrates a teen adopting a family verdict about herself and a parent's belief in her effort lifting her.

subtype: Family verdict about who they will become [Receiver]
passage: "Beta, why didn't you try for the science olympiad?" asked Amma. Karthik, fourteen, shrugged. "Why bother? Everyone says Vikram anna is the brainy one." "Who says?" "Periyappa. Everyone. Since I was small." Amma sat down. "Do you believe it?" Karthik picked at the sofa. "Kind of." Amma was quiet. "I've watched you fix the radio and the fan. That takes patience and brains." Karthik looked up. "Really?" "Really. Try, and see." He nodded slowly. "Maybe next year."

qa.q: What had Karthik fixed that Amma mentioned?
qa.a: The radio and the fan.

qa.q: Why did Karthik not try for the olympiad?
qa.a: He had absorbed the family verdict that his cousin is the brainy one, so trying felt pointless.

qa.q: What did Amma do well?

qa.q: How might Periyappa see his repeated comments?
qa.a: He might think they are just honest comparisons, not seeing how they shape Karthik.

grounding: It shows a teen adopting a repeated family comparison as identity, and a parent's belief starting to lift him.

passage: In a colony garden in Ahmedabad, Arya, five, announced loudly, "I am the doctor!" Her friends were patients. After a while, the others wanted to play shopkeeper. "No," said Arya, "I said I'm the doctor." She kept checking pretend temperatures. Her friends started drifting off to the swings. Arya's face fell, but she stayed with her toy stethoscope. "I'm still the doctor," she whispered, looking at the empty bench.

qa.q: What did Arya announce loudly?
qa.a: She announced she is the doctor.

qa.q: Why did Arya refuse to change the game?
qa.a: Going back on what she had said felt wrong to her, even when it stopped being fun. 😔

qa.q: What could an adult do to help Arya?
qa.a: Show her that she can happily change her mind, maybe by making the doctor visit the shop too.

qa.q: How might her friends see Arya's refusal?
qa.a: They may see her as stubborn and prefer to play elsewhere.

grounding: It shows a child sticking to her announced role even when the game stops being fun.

passage: "I'm the train driver!" said Rehan, five, sitting at the front of the chairs. "Now let's play something else," said his sister. "No, I said I'm the driver." "But it's boring now!" "I said it." Papa looked over. "Rehan, drivers can take a break. Maybe you can be the chef now?" Rehan frowned. "But I said driver." "You can say something new," said Papa. Rehan thought. "Okay. Train driver who cooks." His sister laughed.

qa.q: What role did Rehan first choose?
qa.a: The train driver.

qa.q: Why did Rehan keep saying he was the driver?
qa.a: Having said it out loud, changing felt like breaking his word. 🤔

qa.q: What did Papa do well?
qa.a: He showed Rehan it is okay to say something new, helping him change gently.

qa.q: How might his sister see Rehan's new idea?
qa.a: She found it funny and was probably glad the game could move on.

grounding: It illustrates a child sticking to a spoken role because going back on his word feels wrong.

passage: Teacher's note, KG. In pretend play today, Siya, four, said, "I'm the teacher!" For twenty minutes she kept the role, even when the others asked to play house. When they left, she looked unhappy but did not switch. I asked, "Would the teacher like to visit a house?" Her eyes lit up. She joined the house game as a visiting teacher. It seemed she needed a way to keep her word and still change. I will use this idea again.

qa.q: How long did Siya keep the teacher role?
qa.a: For twenty minutes.

qa.q: Why did Siya look unhappy but not switch?
qa.a: Going back on what she had said felt wrong, even though she wanted to join the others.

qa.q: What did the teacher do well?
qa.a: She offered a way for Siya to keep her role and still join the new game. 👍

qa.q: How might the other children see Siya joining as a visiting teacher?
qa.a: They would probably be happy to have her back in the game.

grounding: It shows a child keeping her announced role and a teacher helping her change without breaking her word.

subtype: Small request opens the way to a bigger one [Actor]
passage: At the hostel study hall, Aryan, eleven, asked the warden, "Can I play the tablet game for just five minutes?" The warden agreed. After five minutes, Aryan said, "Just five more? I'm almost at the next level." The warden nodded. Then: "Can I finish this round, it's only ten minutes?" By the time the warden looked at the clock, it was nearly bedtime, and Aryan's homework was still unopened. The warden sighed. Aryan looked surprised himself.

qa.q: What did Aryan first ask to play?
qa.a: The tablet game for just five minutes.

qa.q: Why did each request feel reasonable to Aryan?
qa.a: After each small yes, one more short request felt like a natural continuation. 😅

qa.q: What could the warden do next time?
qa.a: Set a clear total time at the start and stick to it.

qa.q: How might the warden feel at bedtime?
qa.a: Frustrated with himself for saying yes step by step until the evening was gone.

grounding: It shows a child's small requests growing into the whole evening because each yes made the next feel natural.

subtype: Small request opens the way to a bigger one [Actor]
passage: I'm Mira's older brother. Last night I watched her do this thing with Mum. "Can I watch one cartoon?" Mum said yes. After it ended, Mira said, "Just one more, it's short." Yes again. Mum looked at the clock and said, "How did that happen?" Mira just smiled.

subtype: Small request opens the way to a bigger one [Actor]
passage: Before: On Monday, Kabir, ten, asked his father if he could stay at the park for ten more minutes. His father agreed. passage: "Try the carrot, Ahaan," said Mama. Ahaan, two, pressed his lips shut. "Look, Meera likes it." His cousin Meera crunched a carrot stick and smiled. Ahaan watched her. I have news I haven't told anyone at school. I was selected for the national science contest in Delhi. passage: Caregiver note. Arnav, two, cried when the new helper came today. He clung to me and would not look at her. When I played the song we sing every morning, he calmed and started clapping. The helper sat quietly nearby and sang along. By afternoon he let her hand him a toy. I will keep the same songs and routine while he gets used to her.

qa.q: What did Arnav do when the familiar song played?
qa.a: He calmed and started clapping.

qa.q: Why did Arnav cry when the new helper came?
qa.a: She was unfamiliar, so he did not feel safe with her yet.

qa.q: What is good about the caregiver's plan?
qa.a: Keeping familiar songs and routine helps Arnav feel safe while the helper becomes familiar. 👍

qa.q: How might the helper feel by the afternoon?
qa.a: She may feel encouraged that Arnav let her hand him a toy.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler wary of a stranger and calmed by a familiar song.

passage: At the village temple fair, two-year-old Munni was passed to an aunt she had never met. She stiffened and cried. Her grandmother took her back and sang the same song she sang every evening at home. Munni stopped crying, leaned on her shoulder and watched the crowd quietly. After a while, the aunt sang it too. Munni looked at her, still clinging, but no longer crying.

qa.q: Where was Munni passed to an unknown aunt?
qa.a: At the village temple fair.

qa.q: Why did Munni stop crying when her grandmother sang?
qa.a: The familiar song and person made her feel safe. 🙂

qa.q: What did the aunt do that might help?
qa.a: She sang the same familiar song, helping Munni get used to her.

qa.q: How might the aunt feel when Munni stopped crying?
qa.a: Relieved and hopeful that Munni would warm up to her.

grounding: It shows a toddler wary of an unknown relative and calmed by a familiar song and face.
